than.e: From Middle English than, thanne (“than; then”), from Old English þanne, a variant of þonne (“then; when; than”), from Proto-West Germanic *þannē, an alteration of *þan (“then; than”), from Proto-Germanic *þan (“then; than”), from earlier *þam, from Proto-Indo-European *tóm, accusative masculine of *só (“that”, demonstrative pronoun).
than.g: Used in comparisons, to introduce the basis of comparison.

thank.e: From Middle English thank (“gratitude; expression of gratitude, thanks; attractiveness; commendation, praise; God’s grace; goodwill; merit, reward; mind, thought”), from Old English þanc, þonc (“gratitude; expression of gratitude, thanks; favour, grace; mind, thought; pleasure, satisfaction”), from Proto-Germanic *þankaz (“gratitude.

thankful.e: From Middle English thankful, from Old English þancful, þancfull (“thoughtful, pleasing, agreeable, pleasant, thankful, grateful”), equivalent to thank + -ful.

thanks.e: From Middle English thanks, thankes, from Old English þancas (“thanks”), from Proto-Germanic *þankōs, nominative plural of *þankaz (“thought, gratitude”), from Proto-Indo-European *teng- (“to think, feel”).
thanks.g: Used to express appreciation or gratitude.

thankworthy.e: From Middle English thankworthy, thank-worthy, þankeworþi, probably an alteration (with -y) of earlier Middle English thanke worth, thankworth, þancwurðe (“thankworthy”), from Old English þancwyrþe, þancweorþ (“thankworthy, deserving thanks, acceptable”), equivalent to thank + -worthy.

theatre.e: From Middle English theater, theatre, from Old French theatre, from Latin theatrum, from Ancient Greek θέατρον (théatron, “a place for viewing”), from θεάομαι (theáomai, “to see, watch, observe”).

theft.e: From Middle English theft, thefte, þefte, þefþe, þiefþe, Old English þīefþ, from Proto-West Germanic *þiubīþu, from Proto-Germanic *þiubīþō (“theft”), from *þiubijaną (“to thieve, steal”), equivalent to thieve + -t (abstract nominal suffix).

theirs.e: From Middle English theires, attested since the 1300s. Equivalent to their + -s (compare -'s); formed by analogy to his.
theirs.g: That or those belonging to them; the possessive case of they, used without a following noun.

theme.e: From Middle English teme, from Old French teme, tesme (French thème), from Latin thema, from Ancient Greek θέμα (théma), from τίθημι (títhēmi, “to put, place”), reduplicative from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to put, place, do”) (whence also English do).
theme.g: A subject, now especially of a talk or an artistic piece; a topic.

themselves.g: The reflexive case of they, the third-person plural personal pronoun. The group of people, animals, or objects previously mentioned, as the

thence.e: From Middle English þennes, from þenne + -es (“adverbial ending”), the former from þanan, þanona, from Proto-West Germanic *þananā.
thence.g: From there, from that place or from that time.

thenceforth.e: From Middle English thennesforth, equivalent to thence + forth.

thereabout.e: From Middle English ther-aboute, ther-abouten (“of a place or an object: around there, in its vicinity; surrounding it; nearby, neighbouring; here and there, throughout that place; of an action, matter, etc.: about, concerning; of an amount or distance: approximately, more or less; of time: about then, around that time”).

thereat.e: From Middle English thereat, ther-at, þeratte, þerat, from Old English þǣræt, from Proto-West Germanic *þārat, from Proto-Germanic *þarat, equivalent to there + at.

thereby.e: From Middle English therby, from Old English ðǣrbig, equivalent to there + by.
thereby.g: By it; by that; by that means, or as a consequence of that.

therefore.e: From Middle English therfore, therfor, tharfore, thorfore; synchronically a univerbation of there (pronominal adverb) + for, literally “for that (reason)”. The spelling has been changed due to a reanalysis as there + fore (literally “forward from that; thence”).
therefore.g: Consequently, by or in consequence of that or this cause; referring to something previously stated.

therefrom.e: From Middle English therfrom, þærfrom, þarvram (also as ther-fro, þer-fro, þarfra), equivalent to there + from.

therein.e: From Middle English theryn, ther-inne, þer-in, from Old English þǣrin, þǣrinne, from Proto-West Germanic *þārin, *þārinna, from Proto-Germanic *þarin, *þarinna, equivalent to there + in.
therein.g: in that; in that place; in him/her/it.

thereof.e: From Middle English thereof, therof, ther-of, ther of, from Old English þǣrof; equivalent to there + of.

thereon.e: From Old English þǣron, equivalent to there + on.

thereout.e: From Middle English ther-oute, þer-out, þar-out, þeroute, from Old English þǣrūt and þǣrūte, equivalent to there + out.
thereout.g: Out of it, out from it.

thereto.e: From Middle English therto, from Old English þǣrtō (“thereto”), equivalent to there + to.

thereupon.e: From Middle English therupon, theruppon. Equivalent to there + upon.

therewith.e: c. 1200, from Middle English therwith, from Old English þǣrwiþ (“therewith, in return, in exchange, against”), equivalent to there + with. Parallel with Dutch daarmee, German damit (“therewith”), Swedish därmed (“therewith”), though etymologically different.

thick.e: From Middle English thikke, from Old English þicce (“thick, dense”), from Proto-West Germanic *þikkwī, from Proto-Germanic *þekuz (“thick”), from Proto-Indo-European *tégus (“thick”).
thick.g: Relatively great in extent from one surface to the opposite in its smallest solid dimension.

thicket.e: From Middle English *thikket, from Old English þiccet, from þicce (“thick”) + Old English nominal suffix -et. Latin dūmus (akin to Latin dense).
thicket.g: A dense, but generally small, growth of shrubs, bushes or small trees; a copse.

thickness.e: From Middle English thikkenesse, thiknesse, from Old English þicnes (“thickness, viscosity, density, hardness; obscurity, cloud, darkness; thicket; depth, a thick body, anything thick or heavy”), from Proto-West Germanic *þikkwīnassī (“thickness”), equivalent to thick + -ness.
thickness.g: The property of being thick (in dimension).

thief.e: From Middle English thef, theef, þef, from Old English þēof, from Proto-West Germanic *þeub, from Proto-Germanic *þeubaz.
thief.g: One who carries out a theft.

thieve.e: From Middle English *theven, from Old English þēofian, ġeþēofian, ġeþīefian (“to thieve, steal”).

thigh.e: From Middle English thigh, thegh, thiȝ, theȝhe, þigh, þyȝh, from Old English þēoh, þīoh, from Proto-West Germanic *þeuh, from Proto-Germanic *þeuhą, from Proto-Indo-European *tewk-.
thigh.g: The upper leg of a human, between the hip and the knee.

thin.e: From Middle English thinne, thenne, thünne, from Old English þynne, from Proto-West Germanic *þunnī, from Proto-Germanic *þunnuz (“thin”) – compare *þanjaną (“to stretch, spread out”) – from Proto-Indo-European *ténh₂us (“thin”), from *ten- (“to stretch”).
thin.g: Having little thickness or extent from one surface to its opposite.

thing.e: From Middle English thing, from Old English þing, from Proto-West Germanic *þing, from Proto-Germanic *þingą. The word originally meant "assembly", then came to mean a specific issue discussed at such an assembly, and ultimately came to mean most broadly "an object".
thing.g: That which is considered to exist as a separate entity, object, quality or concept.

think.e: From Middle English thinken, thynken, thenken, thenchen, from Old English þenċan, from Proto-West Germanic *þankijan, from Proto-Germanic *þankijaną (“to think”), from Proto-Indo-European *teng- (“to think, feel, know”).
think.g: To ponder, to go over in one's mind.

think.e: From Middle English thinken, thynken, thenken (also thinchen, thünchen), from Old English þyncan (“to seem, appear”), from Proto-Germanic *þunkijaną (“to seem”).

thinking.e: From Middle English thenkinge, þinkynge, þenkynge, þenchinde, from Old English þenċende, from Proto-Germanic *þankijandz, present participle of *þankijaną (“to think”), equivalent to think + -ing.

third.e: From Middle English thirde, thridde, from Old English þridda, from Proto-Germanic *þridjô, from Pre-Germanic *tretyós, a remodeling of Proto-Indo-European *tr̥tyós.
third.g: The ordinal form of the cardinal number three; Coming after the second.

thirst.e: From Middle English thirst, thurst, from Old English þurst, from Proto-West Germanic *þurstu, from Proto-Germanic *þurstuz, from Proto-Indo-European *ters- (“dry”).
thirst.g: A sensation of dryness in the throat associated with a craving for liquids, produced by deprivation of drink, or by some other cause (such a

thirsty.e: From Middle English thirsty, from Old English þurstiġ, from Proto-West Germanic *þurstug. Equivalent to thirst + -y.
thirsty.g: Needing to drink water or any liquid that can supply water.

thirteen.e: From Middle English thirttene, variant (through metathesis) of thrittene, from Old English þrēotīene, from Proto-Germanic *þritehun, compound of *þrīz (“three”) + *tehun (“teen”). Equivalent to three + -teen.
thirteen.g: The cardinal number occurring after twelve and before fourteen: ten and three.

thirteenth.e: From Middle English thrittenthe, thrittethe, from Old English þrēottēoþa; equivalent to thirteen + -th (ordinal suffix).
thirteenth.g: The ordinal form of the number thirteen.

thirtieth.e: From earlier thirteth, from Middle English thrittithe, threttiþe, thrittyde, from Old English þrītigoþa; equivalent to thirty + -eth. For the modern form, see the etymological notes at twentieth.
thirtieth.g: The ordinal form of the number thirty.

thirty.e: From Middle English thirty, metathetic alternant of thritty, from Old English þrītiġ, þrittiġ (“thirty”), from Proto-Germanic *þrīz tigiwiz (“thirty”, literally “three tens”), equivalent to three + -ty.
thirty.g: The cardinal number occurring after twenty-nine and before thirty-one, represented in Arabic numerals as 30.

thirty-eighth.g: The ordinal form of the number thirty-eight, describing a person or thing in position number 38 of a sequence.

thirty-fifth.g: The ordinal form of the number thirty-five, describing a person or thing in position number 35 of a sequence.

thirty-ninth.g: The ordinal form of the number thirty-nine, describing a person or thing in position number 39 of a sequence.

thirty-seventh.g: The ordinal form of the number thirty-seven, describing a person or thing in position number 37 of a sequence.

thirty-sixth.g: The ordinal form of the number thirty-six, describing a person or thing in position number 36 of a sequence.

thirtyfold.e: From Middle English þrittyfold, thritti fold, from Old English þrītiġfeald (“thirtyfold”), equivalent to thirty + -fold.
thirtyfold.g: thirty times as great, or as many

thistle.e: From Middle English thistel, from Old English þistel, from Proto-West Germanic *þistil, from Proto-Germanic *þistilaz. *þīh- from *teyg-, which is a variant of Proto-Indo-European *(s)teyg- (“to prick”); from this same Proto-Indo-European root comes English stick.
thistle.g: Any of several perennial composite plants, especially of genera Cirsium, Carduus, Cynara, or Onopordum, having prickly leaves and showy flow

thither.e: From Middle English thider, from Old English þider, an alteration (probably by analogy with hider (“hither”)) of earlier þæder (“to there”), from Proto-Germanic *þadrê.

thitherward.e: From Old English þiderweard, equivalent to thither + -ward.

thong.e: From Middle English thong, thwong, thwang, from Old English þwong, þwang (“thong, band, strap, cord, strip of leather; phylactery”), from Proto-West Germanic *þwangi, from Proto-Germanic *þwangiz, *þwanguz (“coercion, constraint, band, clamp, strap”), from Proto-Indo-European *twenk- (“to squeeze, press, pressure”).
thong.g: A narrow strip of material, typically leather, used to fasten, bind, or secure objects.

thorn.e: From Middle English thorn, þorn, from Old English þorn, from Proto-West Germanic *þorn, from Proto-Germanic *þurnaz, from Proto-Indo-European *tr̥nós, from *(s)ter- (“stiff”). Further cognates include Old Church Slavonic трънъ (trŭnŭ, “thorn”), Russian тёрн (tjorn), Polish cierń, Kamkata-viri taňi, tai (“thorn”), Sanskrit तृण (tṛ́ṇa, “grass”).
thorn.g: A modified branch that is hard and sharp like a spike.

thornbush.g: Any of many thorny or spiny shrubs and bushes.

thoroughly.g: In a thorough or complete manner.

though.e: From Middle English though, thogh, from Old Norse *þóh (later þó). Superseded (in most dialects) Middle English thegh, from Old English þēah (“though, although, even if, that, however, nevertheless, yet, still; whether”). Both the Old Norse and Old English are from Proto-Germanic *þauh (“though”).

thought.e: From Middle English thought, ithoȝt, from Old English þōht, ġeþōht, from Proto-West Germanic *þą̄ht, from Proto-Germanic *þanhtaz, *gaþanhtą (“thought”), from Proto-Indo-European *teng- (“to think”).
thought.g: A representation created in the mind without the use of one's faculties of vision, sound, smell, touch, or taste; an instance of thinking.

thousand.e: From Middle English thousend, thusand, from Old English þūsend (“thousand”), from Proto-West Germanic *þūsundi, from Proto-Germanic *þūsundī (“thousand”), (compare Scots thousand (“thousand”), Saterland Frisian duusend (“thousand”), West Frisian tûzen (“thousand”), Dutch duizend (“thousand”), German tausend (“thousand”), Danish tusind (“thousand”).
thousand.g: A numerical value equal to 1,000; ten times a hundred (1 E+3 exactly—in scientific E notation)

thrash.e: From Middle English threschen, thresche, threschyn, threshen, thresshen, tressyn, þreisshe, þresshe, (whence the modern English thresh), from Old English þerscan, þrexan, from Proto-Germanic *þreskaną (“to thresh; to tread”), from Proto-Indo-European *terh₁- (“to rub, turn; to drill, pierce”).

thread.e: From Middle English thred, þred, threed, from Old English þrǣd, from Proto-Germanic *þrēduz, from Proto-Indo-European *treh₁-tu-s, from *terh₁- (“rub, twist”). Non-Germanic cognates include Albanian dredh (“twist, turn”).
thread.g: A cord formed by spinning or twisting together textile fibers or filaments into one or more continuous strands, typically used in needlework

threadbare.e: From Middle English thred-bar, thred-bare (“of cloth, clothing, etc.: worn to such an extent that the warp and weft threads show, shabby, worn-out; (figurative) inadequate, poor”), from thred (“piece of textile twine”) (from Old English þrǣd (“thread”), from Proto-Germanic *þrēduz (“thread.
threadbare.g: Of cloth, clothing, furnishings, etc.: frayed and worn to an extent that the nap is damaged and the warp and weft threads show; shabby, worn

threat.e: From Middle English threte, thret, thrat, thræt, threat, from Old English þrēat (“crowd, swarm, troop, army, press; pressure, trouble, calamity, oppression, force, violence, threat”), from Proto-Germanic *þrautaz, closely tied to Proto-Germanic *þrautą (“displeasure, complaint, grievance, labour, toil”).
threat.g: An expression of intent to injure or punish another.

threat.e: From Middle English threten, from Old English þrēatian (“to press, oppress, repress, correct, threaten”), derived from Proto-Indo-European *trewd- (“to squeeze, push, press”).

threaten.e: From Middle English thretenen, from Old English þrēatnian (“to urge, force, compel”), equivalent to threat + -en.
threaten.g: To make a threat against someone; to use threats.

threatening.e: From Middle English thretenyng, þreteninde, equivalent to threaten + -ing.
threatening.g: Presenting a threat, posing a likely risk of harm.

three.e: From Middle English thre, threo, thrie, thri, from Old English þrī, from Proto-West Germanic *þrīʀ, from Proto-Germanic *þrīz, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes.
three.g: A numerical value equal to 3; the number following two and preceding four.

three-pronged.g: Having three prongs or similar parts; trifurcate.

threefold.e: From Middle English threfold, from Old English þrīfeald. Equivalent to three + -fold.

thresh.e: From Middle English threschen, thresche, threschyn, threshen, thresshen, tressyn, þreisshe, þresshe, from Old English þerscan, þrexan, from Proto-Germanic *þreskaną (“to thresh; to tread”), from Proto-Indo-European *terh₁- (“to rub, turn; to drill, pierce”).
thresh.g: To separate the grain from the straw or husks (chaff) by mechanical beating, with a flail or machinery, or by driving animals over them.

thresher.e: From Middle English threschere; equivalent to thresh + -er. The shark's tail is thought to resemble the implement.

threshing.e: From Middle English thresshyng; equivalent to thresh + -ing.
threshing.g: The process by which something is threshed.

threshold.e: From Middle English threschwolde, threscholde, from Old English þresċold, þerxold, þrexwold (“doorsill, entryway”), from Proto-Germanic *þreskudlaz, *þreskūþlijaz, *þreskwaþluz, from Proto-Germanic *þreskaną, *þreskwaną (“to thresh, (originally) to tread”), from Proto-Indo-European *terh₁- (“to rub, turn”).
threshold.g: The lowermost part of a doorway that one crosses to enter; a sill.

thrice.e: From Middle English thrice, thries (“three times, thrice; a third time; repeated three times”), from earlier thrī, thrīe (“three times, thrice; a third time”) (from Old English þriwa, þreowa) + -es (suffix forming adverbs of time, place, and manner) (from Old English -es (suffix forming adverbs)). The word is cognate with Old Frisian thria ("thrice".

thrive.e: From Middle English thryven, thriven, from Old Norse þrífa (“to seize, grasp, take hold, prosper”), from Proto-Germanic *þrībaną (“to seize, prosper”), from Proto-Indo-European *trep-, *terp- (“to satisfy, enjoy”).
thrive.g: To grow or increase stature; to grow vigorously or luxuriantly; to enjoy a state of excellent health and well-being; to flourish.

throat.e: From Middle English throte, from Old English þrote, þrota, þrotu (“throat”), from Proto-West Germanic *þrotu, from Proto-Germanic *þrutō (“throat”), from Proto-Indo-European *trud- (“to swell, become stiff”).
throat.g: The front part of the neck.

throne.e: From Middle English trone, from Old French trone, from Latin thronus, from Ancient Greek θρόνος (thrónos, “a seat, chair”). Superseded earlier seld (“seat, throne”).
throne.g: An impressive seat used by a monarch, often on a raised dais in a throne room and reserved for formal occasions.
throne.sf: From Ancient Greek θρόνος (thrónos, “a seat, chair”)

throng.e: From Middle English throng, thrang, from Old English þrang, ġeþrang (“crowd, press, tumult”), from Proto-Germanic *þrangwą, *þrangwō (“throng”), from *þrangwaz (“pressing, narrow”), from *þrinhwaną (“to press, to push; to force”), from Proto-Indo-European *trenkʷ- (“to beat; pound; hew; press”).
throng.g: A group of people crowded or gathered closely together.

through.e: From Middle English thurgh, thrugh, thruch, thruh, metathetic variants of thurgh, thurh, from Old English þurh, from Proto-Germanic *þurhw (“through”), from Proto-Indo-European *tr̥h₂kʷe, suffixed zero-grade from *terh₂- (“to pass through”) + *-kʷe (“and”).
through.g: From one side or end of (something) to the other.

through.e: From Middle English thrugh, þrouȝ, throgh, from Old English þrūh (“trough, conduit, pipe; box, chest; coffin, tomb”), from Proto-Germanic *þrūhs (“hollowed-out wood”), from Proto-Indo-European *terh₃u- (“to rub, turn, drill, bore”). Not directly related with German Truhe (“chest”), which belongs to the root of English trough.
through.g: A coffin, sarcophagus or tomb of stone; a large slab of stone laid on a tomb, or in a dry-stone wall from one side to the other; a perpend.

throughout.e: From Old English þurh ūt, equivalent to through + out.
throughout.g: In every part of; all through.

throw.e: From Middle English throwen, thrawen, from Old English þrāwan (“to turn, twist”), from Proto-West Germanic *þrāan, from Proto-Germanic *þrēaną (“to twist, turn”), from Proto-Indo-European *terh₁- (“to rub, rub by twisting, twist, turn”).
throw.g: To hurl; to release (an object) with some force from one’s hands, an apparatus, etc. so that it moves rapidly through the air.

throw.e: From Middle English, from Old English þrāh, þrāg (“space of time, period, while”). Of uncertain origin. Perhaps related to Gothic 𐌸𐍂𐌰𐌲𐌾𐌰𐌽 (þragjan, “to run”).

thrown.e: From Middle English throwen, from Old English þrāwen, ġeþrāwen, from Proto-Germanic *þrēanaz, from Proto-Germanic *þrēaną. Morphologically throw + -n.

thrush.e: From Middle English thrusche, þrusch, þresche, from a combination of Old English þrysċe (from Proto-Germanic *þruskijǭ, a diminutive of Proto-Germanic *þruskō) and Old English þræsċe (from Proto-Germanic *þrauskǭ and/or *þrastuz); all from Proto-Indo-European *trosdos (“thrush”).
thrush.g: Any of numerous species of songbirds of the cosmopolitan family Turdidae, such as the song thrush, mistle thrush, bluebird, and American rob

thrush.e: Uncertain, though likely not related to the "bird" sense of Etymology 1; perhaps compare Icelandic þröstur, Danish torsk, Norwegian trøske. Perhaps also related to Old French fourchette (“frog of a horse's hoof”).
thrush.g: A fungal infection caused by species of genus Candida, affecting the mouth or vagina; candidiasis.

thrust.e: From Middle English þrusten, from Old Norse þrysta, from Proto-Germanic *þrustijaną, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *trewd-.
thrust.g: An attack made by moving the sword parallel to its length and landing with the point.

thumb.e: From Middle English thombe, thoume, thoumbe (“thumb”), from Old English þūma (“thumb”), from Proto-West Germanic *þūmō (“thumb”), from Proto-Germanic *þūmô (“thumb”), from Proto-Indo-European *tūm- (“to grow”). The parasitic ‐b has existed since the late 13th century.
thumb.g: The shortest and thickest digit of the hand that for humans has the most mobility and can be made to oppose (moved to touch) all of the othe

thunder.e: From Middle English thunder, thonder, thundre, thonre, thunnere, þunre, from Old English þunor (“thunder”), from Proto-West Germanic *þunr, from Proto-Germanic *þunraz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ten-, *(s)tenh₂- (“to thunder”).
thunder.g: The loud rumbling, cracking, or crashing sound caused by expansion of rapidly heated air around a lightning bolt.

thunder.e: From Middle English thundren, from Old English þunrian (“to thunder”), from Proto-West Germanic *þunrōn, from Proto-Germanic *þunrōną (“to thunder”).
thunder.g: To produce thunder; to sound, rattle, or roar, as a discharge of atmospheric electricity.

thunderbolt.g: A flash of lightning accompanied by a crash of thunder.

thundering.e: From Middle English thonderynge, þoundryng, equivalent to thunder + -ing.
thundering.g: Of, pertaining to, or accompanied by thunder.

thunderstorm.g: A storm consisting of thunder and lightning produced by a cumulonimbus, usually accompanied with heavy rain, wind, and sometimes hail; and i

thus.e: From Middle English thus, þus, from Old English þus (“thus, in this way, as follows, in this manner, to this extent”), from Proto-West Germanic *þus (“so, thus”), perhaps originally from a variant of the instrumental form of this, related to Old English þȳs (“by this, with this”), Old Saxon thius (“by this, with this”).

thwart.e: From Middle English thwerte, from the adjective thwert (“obstinate, perverse”), from Old Norse þvert, neuter of þverr (“transverse”). It is related to queer; also Proto-West Germanic *þwerh,.
thwart.g: Placed or situated across something else; cross, oblique, transverse.

thyine.g: The fragrant wood of a North African tree (Tetraclinis articulata) in the family Cupressaceae.

thyself.e: From Middle English thy-selfe, thiself, thi-zelf, equivalent to thy + -self.
thyself.g: yourself (as the object of a verb or preposition or as an intensifier); reflexive case of thou
